entries.name: The Caribbean Churches of Slavery and Emancipation
entries.informalName: The Churches of Slavery and Freedom
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). One story of the Baptist, Wesleyan, Native Baptist and mission churches of Jamaica and Demerara. Its window opens in 1815, where the entries on the Moravians and the Baptists end. It closes with the era in 1906.
entries.sourcing: Rich on the missionary side and thin on the side of the enslaved. Almost every text is a missionary's or a mission supporter's. Sharpe's words reach us only through Bleby. The Native Baptists have no words of their own here. This entry does not yet tell the revival of 1860 and 1861 or the rising at Morant Bay in 1865, because no text of those years has been read. Phillippo's account of Liele differs from Liele's own, which is used here.
entries.floorNote: No question for the mission churches. The Native Baptists are not yet assessed, so they enter as a line only.
entries.relationsSummary: George Liele began Baptist work in Kingston before this story. The Moravians, in Jamaica since 1754, have their own entry after 1815. Their chapels and trials are part of this story too.
entries.why: Jamaican Baptists lived through the end of slavery. Samuel Sharpe, a Baptist, promoted a plan to refuse work and was executed in 1832. On the night of 31 July 1838 a Baptist congregation at Falmouth waited for midnight, and next morning it buried a chain, a whip and an iron collar.
entries.teaser: Jamaica and Demerara, 1815 to 1906. Churches among the enslaved, and the dawn in 1838 when a church buried a whip and a chain.
entries.longDescription:
George Liele was a Black Baptist preacher from Georgia. His master, Henry Sharp, had freed him some years before he died. When the British left Georgia, Liele came to Jamaica as an indentured servant, to pay a debt to Colonel Kirkland. Phillippo dates his coming to 1782. Several members of his church followed. In 1813 the Baptist Missionary Society sent John Rowe to work with one of them, Moses Baker, near Falmouth. The Wesleyans had begun work on the island in 1789.

In 1843 a missionary named James Phillippo counted the churches of Jamaica. He found 226 places of worship. Native Baptists held eight or nine of them. They had fourteen ministers.

Samuel Sharpe was a Baptist. The missionary Henry Bleby talked with him in jail. Bleby writes that Sharpe learned from his Bible that whites had no more right to hold Black people in slavery than Black people had to hold whites. Sharpe used prayer meetings on the estates to spread his plan. Those who joined swore not to work again after the Christmas holidays unless they were free. The rising broke out a day or two after Christmas Day, 1831. Bleby writes that once it began, it was beyond Sharpe's control. Sharpe was executed at Montego Bay on 23 May 1832.

The planters blamed the missionaries for the rising. Bleby writes that three Baptist missionaries were tried or charged. A Moravian, Mr. Pfeiffer, faced a court-martial, and a Wesleyan, Mr. Box, was arrested. None of them was found guilty.

On 31 July 1838 the Baptist chapel at Falmouth filled for a night of prayer. The missionary William Knibb pointed to the clock. At the last stroke of midnight he cried, “The monster is dead: the negro is free.” Early next morning a crowd buried a chain, a whip and an iron collar in a coffin, as at a funeral. On 30 November 1838 Knibb wrote to Mr. Sturge about buying land for a village, which he called Birmingham.

In Demerara, now part of Guyana, enslaved people rose in revolt in August 1823. Many in the colony blamed John Smith, who served the London Missionary Society. The court sentenced him to death on 24 November 1823. His memoirist, Edwin Wallbridge, said the charge rested on lies. Smith died on 6 February 1824. The King lifted the sentence, but word of it reached the colony only on 30 March 1824.
voices: Samuel Sharpe — a Baptist of Jamaica, executed at Montego Bay on 23 May 1832 for his part in the rising of Christmas 1831
William Knibb — the missionary at Falmouth who cried at midnight on 31 July 1838, “The monster is dead: the negro is free”
George Liele — a Black Baptist pastor who came from Georgia to Kingston in 1782
John Smith — the London Missionary Society's missionary in Demerara, sentenced to death on 24 November 1823
Henry Bleby — a missionary who lived in Jamaica for seventeen years and wrote of Sharpe from his own talks with him
entries.legacy: In 1843 Phillippo counted 226 places of worship in Jamaica. This entry stops in 1906 and reads no text from later years, so it says nothing about the churches today.

entries.name: Canudos (Belo Monte)
entries.informalName: The Holy Town of the Bahia Backlands
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It is a movement inside popular Catholicism, not a church, so it was tested on four marks. They are a beginning at Canudos in 1893, carriers, a name, and a study. Its window runs from 1893 to the fall of the town in 1897.
entries.sourcing: Moderate, and hostile. The main account is Euclides da Cunha's Os Sertões, in its third edition of 1905. The backlanders speak through a writer who calls the Conselheiro a crude gnostic. The Conselheiro's own sermons were not opened.
entries.floorNote: No question on the record read. Euclides says the Conselheiro attacked the Roman Church. But a friar's report he prints gives the Conselheiro's own answer: his quarrel was with the Republic. No text of the community's own was read.
entries.relationsSummary: It grew out of everyday Catholic life in the backlands of Brazil. A larger entry, on the Catholic church in Latin America, tells that life. It also names Tomóchic in Mexico, a popular movement of the 1890s. This entry claims no link between the two.
entries.why: In 1893 a lay preacher, Antônio Conselheiro, settled his followers in the ruined hamlet of Canudos in Bahia. In 1897 the army besieged it, and it fell. What we know comes mostly from one hostile book.
entries.teaser: Bahia, Brazil, 1893 to 1897 — a lay preacher's holy town, known mostly through one hostile book.
entries.longDescription:
Antônio Conselheiro was a lay preacher of the Bahia backlands. In 1876 he came to Itapicuru de Cima. His followers carried a rough cedar oratory with an image of Christ. At each stop they knelt to pray. They entered the villages singing litanies. Euclides da Cunha wrote the best-known account of him. He was a hostile witness.

In 1893 the Conselheiro was in Bom Conselho when the new town councils posted tax notices. He had the notices burned in the square and preached open rebellion against the laws. That year he reached Canudos, a hamlet in decay. Euclides says it grew fast from then on. A witness says their great wish was to sell what they had and share the money with «o Santo Conselheiro».

Euclides prints prophecies that he says were written in many small notebooks found at Canudos. One reads: «Em 1896 hade rebanhos mil correr da praia para o certão; então o certão virará praia e a praia virará certão.» In English: “In 1896 a thousand flocks will run from the coast to the backlands; then the backlands will become coast and the coast will become backlands” (a rendering). Euclides compares him to old heretics. In that comparison he says the Conselheiro rose against the Roman Church. He says it had lost its glory and obeyed Satan. He calls him «um gnostico bronco», a crude gnostic (a rendering). So his account is not neutral. An officer he quotes saw it the other way. He says the Conselheiro promoted baptisms, weddings, feasts and novenas.

The church acted against him. In 1882 the archbishop of Bahia told his parish priests to forbid their people to gather to hear him. Only the ministers of religion, he wrote, may teach the people. In May 1895 a Capuchin friar, João Evangelista de Monte-Marciano, came to Canudos in the archbishop's name. He came to open a mission and to tell the people to go home. The friar reports the Conselheiro's answer. Under the monarchy, he said, he had let himself be arrested, because he recognized that government. Now he would not, because he did not recognize the Republic (a rendering).

An army order dated 6 September 1897 still tells of shelling the church towers. The last shelling began at dawn on 1 October. Euclides says Canudos fell on the 5th, at dusk. He writes that four defenders were left, an old man, two grown men and a child, with five thousand soldiers raging before them.
voices: Antônio Conselheiro — the lay preacher who led his followers to Canudos in 1893
Euclides da Cunha — the author of Os Sertões, whose hostile account is the main source
entries.legacy: The town was destroyed, and this entry reads no text after 1905. A study named for this movement is Robert M. Levine, Vale of Tears (University of California Press, 1992). It was not opened.

set.teaser: Spanish America and Brazil, 1810 to 1906 — a church that lost its king, waited a generation for Rome to recognize its bishops, and was fought over by every new republic.
set.longDescription:
The Spanish crown had run the church in its American empire under a papal grant, appointing the bishops and collecting the tithes. When the colonies won independence the new republics claimed exactly the same right, and Rome — which had backed the crown — took decades to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut for a generation. What followed was a long fight between liberals and clericals over land, schools, cemeteries and marriage. Sharpest in Mexico, where the Reform laws of the 1850s stripped the church of its property and drove it out of public life, and loudest in Brazil, where two bishops were tried and imprisoned in the 1870s. Rome answered by tightening its grip, importing European clergy and religious orders, rebuilding seminaries on Roman lines, and in 1899 summoning the bishops of the whole continent to Rome for a first Latin American Plenary Council. Underneath all of it the devotional life of ordinary Catholics — confraternities, patronal feasts, pilgrimage shrines, household saints — carried on much as before, often with very few priests.

The rising of 1810 in Mexico began with a priest. He was Miguel Hidalgo, the priest of Dolores. A history printed in 1843 says he began the revolution on 15 September 1810. José María Morelos was the priest of Carácuaro. He left his parish on 25 October 1810. The Inquisition of Mexico later charged that the rebel priest of Dolores, Hidalgo, had sent him to raise troops in the south.

In November 1815 the Inquisition tried Morelos. It called him a degraded priest. It said he had joined «el hereje Cura de Dolores», the heretic priest of Dolores. It said this brought on him the excommunications of some bishops, and its own edicts of 1810 and 1811.

Another popular movement of the 1890s is known from a novel. Heriberto Frías's Tomóchic, in its edition of 1906, tells of a village in Chihuahua. Its people said the name of the Santa de Cabora, Teresa Urrea, with veneration. The novel follows a young officer in the army sent against them, and dates its scenes to October 1892. A novel is not a record of events.

set.longDescription:
Once the first missionary generation had passed, Catholicism in Spanish America settled into being the ordinary religion of whole societies, and its real institutions were local: the cofradías, lay confraternities that maintained an altar or an image, buried their members and paid for their funerals, organized by trade, by parish and often by race — with indigenous confraternities and Black brotherhoods running their own devotional life. Its saints were homegrown: Rose of Lima, canonized in 1671 as the first saint of the Americas, and Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of the same city. Its convents produced writers of the first rank, among them Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz in Mexico, who defended a woman's right to study, and Úrsula de Jesús in Lima, an enslaved woman later freed, whose spiritual diary survives in her own dictated words. Above all it produced Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose shrine at Tepeyac became the devotional center of Mexico and eventually a symbol of Mexican identity itself.

Portuguese America had its own brotherhoods. In Bahia a sermon of 1633 is headed as preached to the brotherhood of the Blacks of a sugar mill, on the feast of St John the Evangelist. It is by the Jesuit António Vieira, in his Maria Rosa Mystica of 1686. In the same book he tells the enslaved workers of a sugar mill that no labor in the world is more like the Cross and Passion of Christ than theirs (a rendering). In 1711 André João Antonil wrote of the mills. He says some masters keep enslaved people for a long time in the cane fields or the mill without baptism. He tells masters not to object when the enslaved choose their own kings. He tells them to let the enslaved keep their morning feasts of Our Lady of the Rosary, of St Benedict and of the patron of the mill chapel. In 1741 Benedict XIV wrote to the bishops of Brazil, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata. His bull Immensa pastorum principis condemned those who enslaved or sold Indians, even baptized ones.

set.longDescription:
The story starts before the Panama congress. James Thomson, an agent of the British and Foreign Bible Society, arrived at Buenos Aires on 6 October 1818. Soon after, he proposed the Lancasterian system of schools to the government. By 1820 the magistrates had engaged him to put the schools of the city and its neighborhood on that plan. In 1821 he sailed round Cape Horn to Chile. There he wrote that he was in every way the servant of the Society. His letters were printed in London in 1827.

The Panama congress met from 10 to 20 February 1916. A committee formed in 1913 organized it. It drew 304 delegates and visitors from 21 nations. Few of them were Latin Americans. Its reports came out in three volumes in 1917. In November 1969 the first Latin American Congress on Evangelization, called CLADE, met in Bogotá. In 1970 the Latin American Theological Fraternity met for the first time, at Cochabamba in Bolivia. Churches met at Huampaní in Peru in 1977 and at Oaxtepec in Mexico in 1978. They meant to form a council of their own. That council, CLAI, was set up at Huampaní in 1982. One source gives 1983. A more conservative body, CONELA, formed as its alternative. Virginia Garrard-Burnett found that Protestants in Guatemala won few converts until the 1960s. Then military power and violence spread. They weakened people's old ties. Indigenous evangelicals in Ecuador organized themselves too. Julián Guamán is an Indigenous author from Ecuador. He dates the start of that organizing to Chimborazo in 1966. The national council of these evangelicals, FEINE, was founded in 1980. Guamán counts more than 1,500 local congregations among them. Susana Andrade studied why Indigenous people in Chimborazo became Protestants. Her book of 2004 sets out to show how Pentecostalism there took on a Quichua form. It took back themes from Indigenous religion. The themes include prayer, the interpretation of dreams and baptism in lagoons.

Euclides also writes that the Conselheiro attacked the Roman Church ('ella perdeu a sua gloria e obedece a Satanaz'). The floorNote of the Canudos row says so plainly. Mark should rule whether Section A stays 'no question'.

RECORD vs RAW TEXT: the record says Euclides took the prophecies from a footnote 'not checked'. The footnote was read: it says the prophecies were written in many small notebooks found at Canudos, copied from one belonging to the commander-in-chief's secretary. The row says only that they were in notebooks found there.

RECORD vs RAW TEXT: the record's Hidalgo and Morelos evidence (Bustamante) holds nothing on Morelos and little on Hidalgo's acts. The line instead rests on the Inquisition's case papers of 1815 in G. García's edition (Documentos inumeros, tomo XII; 1907), a public-domain text opened raw, which the record does not cite. The edition is dated 1907 although the documents are of 1815; Mark may want to rule that a 1907 edition of 1815 papers is acceptable evidence in an era 9 row. The Inquisition is a hostile source and the row says so.
